cards.front: Why are a human sperm and an egg built so differently?
cards.back: Each cell is adapted to its job. The **sperm** is small and mobile so it can reach and enter the egg. The **egg** is large and still, storing nutrients and carrying protective layers for the early embryo.
cards.hint: Think about the job each cell has in reproduction.

cards.back: Each gamete has $23$ chromosomes, so when a sperm and egg fuse the **zygote** has $46$ chromosomes, the full set. If gametes were diploid, the chromosome number would double each generation.
cards.hint: Consider which two cells meet to form a zygote.

cards.front: What is the correct order of the four steps that take a sperm from swimming to fertilising an egg?
cards.back: 1) The tail moves the sperm towards the egg, powered by ATP from the midpiece. 2) The acrosome releases enzymes that digest a path through the outer layers. 3) The sperm membrane fuses with the egg membrane. 4) Cortical granules release enzymes that change the zona pellucida and block other sperm.
cards.hint: Start with how the sperm gets close to the egg.

cards.back: A **gamete** is a haploid sex cell, such as a sperm or an egg, that joins with another gamete at fertilisation.

cards.front: Which type of division produces gametes?
cards.back: **Meiosis** produces gametes. It halves the chromosome number and normally makes four genetically different cells.
The **acrosome** is a membrane-bound sac at the tip of the sperm head. It contains digestive enzymes that can break down the layers around an egg.
cards.hint: Look at where it sits on the sperm head.

cards.front: Why does the sperm midpiece contain many mitochondria?
cards.back: Mitochondria release energy by aerobic respiration to make ATP. The ATP powers the movement of the tail.
cards.hint: Think about what the tail needs in order to move.

cards.front: Why does a sperm have very little cytoplasm?
cards.back: Little cytoplasm keeps the sperm light so it can swim easily. The trade-off is that it carries almost no food store.
cards.hint: Compare with the amount of cytoplasm in an egg.

cards.back: The **zona pellucida** is a jelly-like layer of glycoproteins surrounding the cell surface membrane of a mammalian egg.
cards.hint: Think about what lies just outside the egg membrane.

cards.back: **Cortical granules** are vesicles lying just beneath the egg cell surface membrane. They contain enzymes that are released after a sperm enters.

cards.front: Why is it wrong to describe an egg as diploid?
cards.back: An egg is **haploid**, so its nucleus holds $23$ chromosomes. The $46$ chromosomes only appear in the zygote after fusion with a sperm.
cards.hint: Count the chromosomes in the egg nucleus before fertilisation.

cards.front: What would happen if cortical granule enzymes failed to act after a sperm entered?
cards.back: Extra sperm could enter the egg, so the zygote would end up with too many chromosomes.
